They're closely related, often used interchangeably in casual conversation, but technically different in when and how they affect geometry.

Height map: a grayscale image where pixel brightness represents elevation (white = high, black = low). By itself it's just data, a 2D image. It becomes geometry only when something samples it and moves vertices accordingly, most commonly in terrain generation.

Displacement map: the general term for any texture used to physically move vertex positions, not just up/down elevation, but along any direction (usually the surface normal). A height map is technically one specific type of displacement map, restricted to vertical (normal-direction) movement based on grayscale intensity.
Key practical difference: where it applies.
Height maps are almost always associated with terrain, flat base mesh, sample the map, push vertices up along Y. Simple, single-axis.
Displacement maps are more general, used on any mesh (a sphere, a face, a rock), pushing each vertex along its own normal direction, which varies across the surface, not just straight up.

Also worth knowing: displacement mapping actually changes vertex positions (real geometry, real silhouette, real shadows), which is different from normal mapping or bump mapping. Those fake the appearance of detail using lighting tricks without changing the actual mesh, cheaper but the silhouette stays flat, and it falls apart at grazing angles.

For generative art work, when you're pushing vertices around with noise or an image, you're doing displacement mapping. "Height map" is just the specific case when your source data is a simple 2D image applied to a flat plane.

Video games often use atmospheric models to improve scale. A mountain 20 kilometers away should not appear as sharp as a nearby tree. Atmospheric scattering makes large worlds feel believable because the atmosphere itself communicates distance.
Planet rendering uses even more advanced atmospheric models. The atmosphere becomes a volume surrounding the planet, and the renderer computes light paths through it. This produces:
Games such as Microsoft Flight Simulator and No Man's Sky rely heavily on atmospheric scattering.
Atmospheric effects are also important for art direction. A game may intentionally use:
Thus, atmosphere is not merely realism; it is also mood.
From a rendering perspective, atmospheric models usually sit near the end of the pipeline:
The atmosphere is a gigantic transparent volume between the world and the camera.
Everything you see is filtered through that volume. The farther an object is, the more atmosphere lies between it and the viewer, and therefore the stronger the atmospheric effect becomes.

For real-time graphics, atmospheric rendering often represents one of the largest contributors to realism because it affects the entire image simultaneously. A scene with simple geometry but good atmospheric scattering frequently appears more convincing than a highly detailed scene rendered in perfectly clear air.

, the renderer takes each visible object, runs its vertex shader, rasterizes triangles, runs the fragment shader, computes material response, applies lights, and writes the final color to the framebuffer. Conceptually, it is: geometry → material → lighting → final pixel. This is the most direct mental model: “draw this object with these lights.” LearnOpenGL describes forward rendering as rendering each object and lighting it against the scene’s light sources, object by object. The cost grows quickly because each rendered fragment may need to consider many lights. (
The simple cost model for forward rendering is roughly
objects × pixels × relevant lights × material cost

. That is not an exact formula, but it captures the problem. If one object is affected by eight lights, its fragment shader may evaluate eight lights. If another object overlaps it but loses the depth test later, some work may have been wasted. Modern GPUs can reduce this with early depth testing, depth pre-passes, light culling, and Forward+, but classic forward rendering is still naturally tied to “shade while drawing the object.”

. In forward rendering, lighting is coupled to object drawing. In deferred rendering, the renderer first answers “what surface is visible at this screen pixel?” and only then answers “how is that visible surface lit?” That is why deferred rendering is often strong in scenes with many dynamic lights. Once the G-buffer contains only the topmost visible surface per pixel, lighting can be computed once per visible pixel, rather than repeatedly for every object fragment that might contribute. LearnOpenGL notes that deferred rendering can optimize scenes with large numbers of lights and that the G-buffer contains the actual fragments that survive depth testing. (
forward rendering is like painting a wall object by object, fully finishing each object as you paint it

. Deferred rendering is like first producing a detailed “surface description map” of the final image, then doing lighting as a separate operation over that map. The first approach is simpler and direct. The second approach is more architectural: it creates intermediate data so later passes can make smarter decisions.

. Standard deferred rendering only stores the topmost visible surface in the G-buffer. Transparent rendering needs multiple layers, ordering, blending, refraction, and partial visibility. A single G-buffer pixel cannot naturally represent “glass in front of smoke in front of metal in front of a wall.” Because of that, real engines commonly use
forward rendering for transparent objects, particles, hair, water, glass, and special materials

is another classic pain point. In forward rendering, multisample anti-aliasing fits the pipeline naturally because geometry coverage and shading happen together. In deferred rendering, the renderer has to store and resolve multiple samples of G-buffer data, which is more complicated and memory-heavy. LearnOpenGL mentions that MSAA “no longer works” in the simple deferred model and requires workarounds. Unity’s comparison table also marks anti-aliasing support differently between forward and deferred in the built-in pipeline. (

problem. In forward rendering, every object can have a highly custom shader. In deferred rendering, all visible opaque surfaces usually need to encode their material properties into a shared G-buffer schema. That schema must be broad enough for the engine’s material system but compact enough to avoid huge bandwidth costs. This is why deferred renderers often fit standardized PBR material models very well, but exotic shading models need special handling, extra buffers, material IDs, stencil routing, or separate forward passes.
is: submit opaque objects, shade them with their lights, write final color, then submit transparent objects, particles, UI, and post-processing. A simplified pipeline for

is: submit opaque objects into the G-buffer, run lighting over the G-buffer, compose the lit scene, then render transparent and special objects forward, then apply post-processing. Real engines are more complex, but this captures the architectural split.

A renderer may use deferred for opaque world geometry, forward for transparent objects, special forward passes for hair or water, clustered lighting for both forward and deferred paths, compute passes for tiled lights, and screen-space buffers regardless of the main path. Unity’s URP, for example, exposes both Forward and Deferred rendering paths, and its deferred path stores material attributes in a G-buffer layout with fields such as albedo, specular/metallic information, normal, smoothness, emissive/GI/lighting, and related data. A modern alternative worth knowing is

in many discussions. It keeps the forward material model but adds a light-culling prepass. The screen is divided into tiles, or the camera frustum is divided into 3D clusters, and each tile or cluster gets a compact list of relevant lights. Then forward shaders evaluate only that local light list. This preserves many forward-rendering advantages while solving much of the “too many lights” problem.
